pr_title: validate: ignore providers with no configuration
pr_body:
This PR changes the behavior of `terraform validate` so that provider schema validation is bypassed if the user does not supply provider configuration. The strategy is pretty simple: if the provider config validates against any empty schema, consider it valid. In other words, if the configuration is completely empty, skip validation against the provider schema. Otherwise, proceed to fetch the provider schema, build the configuration against it, and report errors as usual.

I could particularly use guidance on any side effects this might have, particularly if validation is used ahead of other steps that might depend on current behavior.

What follows is a bit of background on the different variations on provider configuration I'm expecting.

<hr>

The below provider configurations, many of which @apparentlymart described in https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/21408#issuecomment-495746582, can become valid at runtime but will currently raise errors during a `terraform validate`.

#### Child Module

When authoring a child module, it's useful to `terraform validate`, particularly because it interacts with provider plugins. It's Terraform's "compile" step—we might still have runtime errors, but we're using types correctly.

1. Inherited providers

No provider declared, the default instance of this provider will be inherited from the parent

```tf
resource "aws_instance" "foo" {
  instance_type = "t3.nano"
  ami = "abc-123"
}
```

2. Proxy provider blocks

```tf
provider "aws" {
  alias = "foo"
}

resource "aws_instance" "foo" {
  provider = aws.foo
  instance_type = "t3.nano"
  ami = "abc-123"
}
```

`foo` is declared but not configured, and we expect the caller to pass `providers = { aws.foo = ... }`.

3. Fully configured provider blocks

```tf
resource "aws_organizations_account" "account" {
  name = "my_new_account"
  email = "john@doe.org"
  role_name = "OrganizationAccountAccessRole"
}

provider "aws" {
  alias = "account"

  assume_role {
    role_arn = "arn:aws:iam:${aws_organizations_account.account.id}:role/${aws_organizations_account.account.role_name}"
  }
}

resource "aws_instance" "foo" {
  provider = aws.foo
  instance_type = "t3.nano"
  ami = "abc-123"
}
```

The module inherits a provider in order to dynamically configure another provider (here in a new AWS account). Or perhaps the module just accepts variables and then configures the provider, though this should be uncommon.

4. Unnecessarily declared provider blocks

I included this as an edit, because my change will end up handling them. 

```tf
provider "aws" {
  version = "~> 2"
}

resource "aws_instance" "foo" {
  instance_type = "t3.nano"
  ami = "abc-123"
}
```

In a child module, this is unnecessary and will lead to weird bugs when the user inevitably doesn't set `providers = { aws = aws }` once and the child provider has none of the configuration the module is supposed to inherit. 

Terraform could warn on version-only provider blocks in child modules, probably even in validate, I'd be up for working on that in a separate PR.

### Root Module

All the same uses of `terraform validate` apply to root modules. The provider configuration is more likely to be populated, but isn't necessarily so. 

1. Implicit provider

```tf
resource "aws_instance" "foo" {
  instance_type = "t3.nano"
  ami = "abc-123"
}
```

The configuration doesn't declare a provider.

2. Declared empty provider

```tf
provider "aws" {}

resource "aws_instance" "foo" {
  instance_type = "t3.nano"
  ami = "abc-123"
}
```

The provider is declared but has no configuration. This configuration is valid at runtime if environment variables satisfy the required provider configuration. And I believe it is also required to enable provider passing to a module, e.g. `providers = { aws.foo = aws }` as in the case 2 for child modules.

My experience as a Terraform user has been that writing provider configuration is a rarity and I'm able to rely on environment variables almost exclusively. This has translated nicely to Terraform Cloud (Enterprise in my case) where we've wired up the `tfe_workspace` and `tfe_variable` resources in a module that distributes credentials for ~10 providers to the workspaces that need them such that the Terraform configuration repos/directories have zero provider configuration required.

3. Configured providers

```tf
provider "aws" {
  region = "us-west-2"
}

resource "aws_instance" "foo" {
  instance_type = "t3.nano"
  ami = "abc-123"
}
```

The provider supplies at least partial configuration. At this point I think we have to validate what we're given. If provider authors want to have required non-credential fields, they'll need to make the credentials fields optional, and validate in the `ConfigureFunc`. And even then, there are good reasons to make credentials optional (https://github.com/terraform-providers/terraform-provider-datadog/pull/474).

Even the somewhat odd required `features {}` block in the Azure provider would seem to be compatible with this stance:

https://www.terraform.io/docs/providers/azurerm/index.html#example-usage

This may not entirely satisfy users who'd like all required fields to be optional, but I don't see how we can accomplish that without throwing away legitimate errors. Azure is a good example there, `features {}` is required, it would be wrong for `terraform validate` to preempt or discard an error. Required fields are often credentials which probably use `schema.EnvDefaultFunc`, but there's no simple/safe heuristic Terraform could use to ignore those errors.

Closes #21408

Hey @pselle, merged with master! Relocated this logic to its new location, but the change itself remains the same.

To my note above:

> I could particularly use guidance on any side effects this might have, particularly if validation is used ahead of other steps that might depend on current behavior.

I noticed that `ConfigureProvider` makes no assumptions that the configuration has already been validated, since it implicitly re-validates as part of evaluating the config:

https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/master/terraform/node_provider.go#L95-L100

So this wouldn't have a side effect of causing a `ConfigureFunc` to panic because a required attribute is missing. Or in other words, it should only affect the `validate` command.

> I noticed that ConfigureProvider makes no assumptions that the configuration has already been validated, since it implicitly re-validates as part of evaluating the config:

The section you've highlighted shows that there's no check to ensure that `resp.Provider.Block` isn't nil. The validation request still happens here: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/master/terraform/node_provider.go#L122-L128 within the `ConfigureProvider` method.

To say, I've read through to make sure the validation is still happening -- the thing that is not happening is the nil check, which is in the `ValidateProvider` function with a note that "it should never happen in real code" so I'm inclined, if we didn't run into any issues in the tests, to add that nil check when it's warranted by a real use case.

With that, this is looking merge-able to me, provided you rebase the PR (sorry about that 😅 ).
Appreciate all the notes! Will address everything and fix the conflict this week.
Ok, took me a bit longer than expected to get back to this, but should be ready! All comments addressed, and the conflict is resolved.

There was a meaningful conflict with #27261, which added improved error handling when a `provider` block is not defined. I've run into that before, particularly in Terraform Cloud, so I was glad to see that improvement.

In order to resolve the conflict, I made the following changes here:

* Removed the conditional sourceless diagnostic from `ValidateProvider`, since the earlier check against an empty schema added here makes that an unreachable branch
* Modified the validate tests so that rather than a missing required attribute there is a type mismatch
* Added test with a missing required attribute which should not result in errors

`ConfigureProvider` still retains all the new behavior.

Hi @plum117! Thanks for reporting this.

Indeed, the documentation is missing a note to say that `-check-variables=false` applies only to Terraform v0.11 and earlier.

The option is removed from Terraform v0.12 because `terraform validate` now _always_ behaves as if this were `false`: validation means "check that the syntax is valid and types/values are being used correctly", which means validation reports on whether the module is valid _regardless of_ particular variable values. `terraform plan`, on the other hand, validates a particular _run_ of Terraform, with a particular set of variable values, data source results, etc.

So with that said, for any situation where you would've run `terraform validate -check-variables=false` in Terraform 0.11 you can just run `terraform validate` in Terraform 0.12 to get an equivalent result.

We'll get the documentation updated to mention that `-check-variables` applies only to Terraform v0.11 and prior. Thanks again!

Thanks for the info

I tried `terraform validate` on v0.12.0 compare to `terraform validate -check-variables=false` on `0.11.14` but it does not do the same behavior. Before, it was actually not checking variables, however now it expect to have the variable "region" which is actually defined in projects using our module.

Thanks for the additional context, @plum117.

Given the error message you saw here, it looks like you've found a bug in `terraform validate`. Could you share the relevant parts of the configuration you're using for testing, so that we can try to reproduce it? 

From the wording of the message it sounds like the problem may be inside a `module` block rather than about a top-level variable. If that's true, then Terraform is detecting that there's a missing `region` argument inside a module block, which is something different than checking whether a `region` variable on the _root_ module was set. If Terraform 0.11.14 wasn't catching that, then I think it was a bug in Terraform _0.11.14_, because `-check-variables=false` was only supposed to ignore the [root variable assignment mechanisms](https://www.terraform.io/docs/configuration/variables.html#assigning-values-to-root-module-variables), not child module calls.

Hi @rquadling!

I'm going to answer your terminology questions first because I think that'll make my subsequent answer easier to follow:
* A _module_ is the combination of all of the `.tf` files in a particular directory, which has input variables, output values, resources and various other constructs that all share a single namespace.
* A _configuration_ is what we call the tree of modules, starting at some root module and including all of its descendent modules. I think this is what you're referring to when you say "a plan".
* A _plan_, in Terraform's usual terminology, is a set of specific actions (create, read, replace, update, or delete) that Terraform must take in order to make the real remote system match an updated configuration.

When it comes to re-usable modules that are used only as child modules, the developer of such a module will be working on it outside of the context of any particular caller, so _during development_ the child module is treated like a root module of a configuration: check out its VCS repository separately, run `terraform init` inside it, and then run `terraform validate`. A key reason why `terraform validate` does not require the root variables to be set is so that a child module can be validated for correctness in isolation, rather than in the context of a particular parent module calling it.

Running `terraform plan` in this context is also possible if you want to test the effect of the module, though it'll be necessary to use `-var` and `-var-file` options on the command line to provide values for the module's input variables.

---

For modules that have complex dependencies that also need to be created, a more advanced pattern is to create a `test` subdirectory under the module and place under that one or more root modules that exist only for easier testing of the module.

You can see that, for example, in the `test/simple` subdirectory of [a work-in-progress module I've been developing](https://github.com/terraformk8s/terraform-aws-eks-cluster): the module requires an EC2 VPC and one or more subnets to exist, so that test module declares some suitable objects and passes them into the module, and so my development workflow is to run `terraform init`, `terraform plan` and `terraform apply` from inside that `test/simple` directory, so I don't have to manually create a suitable VPC and subnets each time I want to test changes to the module.

I don't have any automated CI set up for that repository right now, but if I did I'd run `terraform init && terraform validate` in both the root directory to validate the module, and in the `test/simple` directory to test that the module is accepting the arguments provided to it in that test configuration.

Ahh, okay! I was going down the wrong path because we were talking about `-check-variables`, and so I was assuming that we were talking about variables rather than providers, but indeed I can see now that the "variables" in that name was misleading: provider configuration is the important thing here.

Terraform is in a bit of a tough spot here because it's trying to validate the provider configurations against the provider schema, and the provider schema says `region` is required, but yet as you say normally that setting would be coming from a parent module, so it's normal for it to not be set in this isolated-shared-module situation.

I think the trick here will be to introduce a new subtlety into the validation: the `terraform validate` command should only validate a provider configuration if there's an explicit `provider` block. If there's no explicit block (and thus an empty configuration is implied), `terraform validate` would skip validating the configuration and leave that for `terraform plan` to check. This is acceptable because `terraform validate` doesn't actually need to configure the provider itself, so (unlike with other commands) skipping a provider with an implied configuration won't prevent other validation from completing.

There are a few tricks to this we need to watch out for:
* In a child module, it's valid to have a `provider` block which contains _only_ an `alias` argument, which is a "proxy configuration block" declaring that an aliased provider must be passed from the parent module. `terraform validate` must therefore treat this as if the provider block wasn't present at all, which unfortunately means that `terraform validate` won't be able to catch when a _non-proxy_ aliased provider block is missing all of its arguments, but I think that's an okay compromise because `terraform plan` will catch it.
* In Terraform 0.11 and prior, a `provider` block containing only a `version` argument was commonly used to create a version constraint without configuration. In this case there is an alternative way in Terraform v0.12, so we don't need to make an exception for this case but should be sure that the documentation is clear that `version` inside a `provider` block is deprecated in favor of the new separate version constraint construct:

  ```hcl
  terraform {
    required_providers {
      aws = ">= 2.12.0"
    }
  }
  ```

For the moment, the workaround I'd suggest is to set the `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` environment variable so that the Terraform AWS provider can treat that as a placeholder value to pass validation. We'll do something like the above in a future release to avoid that requirement.

```yaml
image: hashicorp/terraform:light

  docker: true

definitions:
  steps:
    - step: &terraform-validate
        name: Terraform validate
        caches:
          - docker

          - echo -e '\nprovider "azurerm" { \n features {} \n}' >> versions.tf
          - terraform init -backend=false
          - terraform validate

  default: &default
    - step: *terraform-validate
```
